newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS - Mexican consumption disappointing in Q1.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Mexican consumption disappointing in Q1.

text.p: Mexico's consumer spending grew a disappointing two percent in the first quarter, clouding the economic recovery and the sales outlook for some of Mexico's leading firms, analysts said on Thursday.

In a quarterly report on supply and demand of goods and services in Q1, that provides a detailed breakdown of the 5.1 percent gross domestic product growth during that period, private consumption grew 2 percent, compared with 4.4 percent growth in Q4 1996.

"This supports the theme...that consumer spending is the weak reed in this recovery," said Ernest Brown, economist at Morgan Stanley Dean Witter in New York, noting that private demand is the most important component of economic growth.
"It is in line with the pattern that we saw in the prior quarter. The consumer is reasonably close to being supine and everything else is kicking in," Brown said.
He had predicted a four percent growth in private demand in the first quarter, and other analysts had also over-estimated the consumer rebound.

On the positive side, he noted that investment spending, or capital formation, was up 18.1 percent, which suggested firms were building plants and buying machinery, boding well for the future, even though Mexicans in general were not yet buying with a vengeance.
"The center of gravity (in the report) was more toward the investment and export side. The consumer was weaker than where we were guessing.".
Since Mexico begun to recover from its 1994-5 economic crisis by placing heavy reliance on a vibrant export sector, domestic consumption has constantly lagged.
Last year, the supply and demand figures for much of the year painted a rosier picture of demand than many analysts had predicted, and than seperate retail and wholesale data were suggesting.

But the 1996 demand figures were revised down last December and analysts say they are now painting a fairer -- if gloomier -- picture. "They've given us a very realistic number for private consumption," said Gray Newman, economist at HSBC James Capel.

He confessed he was surprised at the modest increase, and pointed out that the slow growth in demand was particularly poignant because most major Mexican companies listed on the stock market are consumer-related.
The demand data "are reaffirming our view that while we have a decent recovery, the consumer is clearly lagging," Newman said.
He noted that economic data were giving very mixed signals about the strength of the recovery at the moment. On the one hand, industrial production, exports and job growth were vibrant.
On the other, wage growth remained in the doldrums, which stifles consumer demand, he added.

"The amount of workers who earn less than one minimum wage remains at a fairly high level compared to 1994," he said, referring to the year before the government devalued the peso and plunged the economy into its worst recession in modern history.
